questions.q: Define Per Capita Income of a state and write the formula used to calculate it.
questions.a: Per Capita Income (PCI) of a state = Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) of the state ÷ Total Population of the state. Unit: Rupees per person per year. A wrong answer (e.g., using GDP instead of NSDP, or dividing population by income) reveals the student confuses national vs state aggregates or inverts the ratio, a common error in board exams when rushing.

questions.q: State A has NSDP of ₹12 lakh crore and population 8 crore. State B has NSDP of ₹4 lakh crore and population 1 crore. Which state has higher Per Capita Income? Explain why total NSDP alone cannot determine this.
questions.a: State A PCI = ₹12,00,000 crore / 8 crore = ₹1,50,000. State B PCI = ₹4,00,000 crore / 1 crore = ₹4,00,000. State B has higher PCI despite lower total NSDP. A wrong answer (choosing State A) shows the student equates larger total income with higher average income, ignoring the population denominator — the exact trap CBSE sets in comparison questions.

questions.q: Calculate the Per Capita Income of a state with NSDP ₹9,50,000 crore and population 19 crore. If the population grows by 2% next year while NSDP grows by 5%, what will be the new PCI? (Round to nearest rupee.)
questions.a:
Step 1: Current PCI = 9,50,000 / 19 = ₹50,000.
Step 2: New NSDP = 9,50,000 × 1.05 = 9,97,500 crore.
Step 3: New Population = 19 × 1.02 = 19.38 crore.
Step 4: New PCI = 9,97,500 / 19.38 ≈ ₹51,470.
A wrong answer (e.g., adding percentages) reveals the student treats PCI growth as sum of growth rates, not understanding PCI = NSDP/Pop requires recomputation.

questions.q: Two states have the same Per Capita Income of ₹1,00,000. State X has high inequality (top 10% earn 50% of income); State Y has low inequality. Can PCI alone tell us which state's *typical* citizen is better off? Why or why not?
questions.a: No. PCI is a mean average; it hides distribution. In State X, the median income (typical citizen) could be far below ₹1,00,000 due to concentration at the top. In State Y, median is closer to the mean. A wrong answer ("yes, PCI is same so well-being is same") shows the student doesn't grasp that PCI ignores inequality — a key limitation CBSE tests in case-based questions.

questions.q: "Goa has higher Per Capita Income than Kerala, so Goa is more developed." Evaluate this statement using the concept of development you have studied.
questions.a: The statement is incomplete. Development includes health, education, and public facilities (literacy, IMR, life expectancy) — not just income. Kerala has lower PCI but higher HDI due to better social indicators. A wrong answer (agreeing solely on PCI) reveals the student treats income as the only development goal, contradicting the multi-dimensional view taught in this chapter (nodes 001, 002, 005).

questions.q: Design a 3-step method for a student to compare the economic development of any two Indian states using only government-published data (NSO, RBI, Census). Specify the exact data points needed and the calculation.
questions.a:
Step 1: Obtain latest NSDP (at current prices) for both states from RBI's "State-wise GDP" tables.
Step 2: Obtain latest population estimates for both states from Census/NSO projections.
Step 3: Calculate PCI = NSDP / Population for each; rank states by PCI. Also note year of data for comparability.
A poor answer (vague steps, missing data sources, or using GDP instead of NSDP) shows the student cannot operationalise the concept with real Indian data sources — a skill CBSE expects in competency questions.
